Draft-for-the-napkin-ring.title: Draft for the napkin ring
Draft-for-the-napkin-ring.content:
You have surely seen a napkin ring before. It might’ve been at a party, wedding, or fancy restaurant.

A napkin ring is formed by drilling a cylindrical hole through the center of a sphere.
The interesting thing happens when we try to find an equation describing the volume of such a simple shape.
The napkin ring theorem shows that if we drill a cylindrical hole through the center of any sphere with some radius r_{s}, the volume of the resultant shape will depend only on its height regardless of the magnitude of r_{s}.
V_{b}= \boxed{\frac{\pi h_{b}^3}{6}}
For example; imagine we have two spheres. One has a radius r_{s,1}  and the other r_{s,2} where r_{s,1} = 10r_{s,2} . If we drill appropriately sized cylindrical holes on both in such a way that the resultant pair of bands have the same height, they would have the exact same volume.
Conceptually, we can understand the cylinder to be something like a cookie cutter instead of a hole. This allows us to inspect more closely the interaction between the sphere and the cylinder.

The sphere has some radius r_s, which means that the distance from the origin to some point P in the surface of the sphere will always be the radius r_s. Moreover, the distance from the origin to the north pole is also r_s, which gives us that the total height of a sphere is h_s = 2r_s. This remains true for any sphere.
In the case of the napkin ring, its height will be less than the height of the original sphere so that h_b < 2r_s.
(note that we used the subscript “b” for simplicity. “b” also stands for “bead” which is another object with the same shape)
Let’s take a look at the napkin ring.

Before continuing, let us clearly define our current variables:
r_{s}= \text{Radius of the sphere}, \qquad r_{c} = \text{Radius of the cylinder}  
h_{b}=\text{Height of napkin ring}
How do we find the volume of the napkin ring?
You might be tempted to try subtracting the volume of the cylinder from that of the sphere to get the volume of the bead.  Although it sounds logical and it is a good try, you must remember that the cookie cutter is not really the volume that we remove from the sphere but rather just the tool used.
If we observe the napkin ring closely, we can see that the volume removed is not really a standard cylinder. It is more like a cylinder with two domes.
We will be using the tools that calculus provides to us. Integrating by means of the washer method will help us derive a formula that describes the volume of the napkin ring.
How does the washer method works?
The washer method works conceptually by subtracting the area of a smaller circle with radius r_i from the area of a bigger circle of radius r_o. Then we multiply by its thickness h_{w}

The washer method is a perfect match for this scenario because it uses an inner radius r_i and an outer radius r_o.

To calculate the volume of a washer, we subtract the area of the inner circle from the area of the outer circle:
 A_{w}= \pi r_{o}^2 - \pi r_{i}^2 = \boxed{ \pi(r_{o}^2 - r_{i}^2)}
Then we just need to multiply by its thickness:
 
V_{w} \approx (\pi(r_{o}^2 - r_{i}^2)) \cdot h_{w}

The idea is to create a series of washers whose inner and outer radii match the cross-section of the napkin ring at each height. The number of washers used depends on the thickness h_{w}. Then, we will calculate the volume of each individual washer and add them up.
The following example uses a sphere to show how the washer method works conceptually.

By using only a few thick washers, we are able to have a rough approximation of the sphere. Because the washers don’t follow closely the sphere’s curved boundary, some regions are missed while others extend out of the sphere.
Check out what happens as we decrease the thickness more and more.

As the washers become thinner, they follow more precisely the curved boundary, so the total washer volume approaches the sphere’s actual volume. Therefore, as h_{w}  approaches zero our approximation becomes more accurate.
Using the washer method to derive the volume formula.
The following section is more mathematical, but it follows from the concepts that we previously explained. Although it might be a bit more confusing, follow along to see how the magic happens.
Let r_{s} be the radius of a parent sphere and r_{c} the radius of the drilled hole.
Place the napkin ring  in a three-dimensional coordinate space, with its center at the origin (0,0,0).
The z-axis passes vertically through the drilled hole.
The cylinder and sphere are centered around the z-axis.
Horizontal washers are perpendicular to the z-axis.
The z-axis will be chosen as the vertical axis.
Let us begin by drawing a cross-section of the napkin ring in the z x-plane:

La-certidumbre-de-una-mañana-común.title: La certidumbre de una mañana común
La-certidumbre-de-una-mañana-común.content:
Comenzando por el aburrimiento,
seguido de una flojera de existir,
y luego un desliz hacia los sueños de una mente despierta,
es en este cúmulo de ideas donde una vez más se amasa una salida,
una poderosa imaginación que desea un día un poquito mejor.
Aunque lo contrario fuera deseado,
el recuento del pasado es esperado.
Incluso habiendo llegado a la esperanza,
eventualmente se aterriza en una manada de memorandos.
Lo que fue y lo que no fue en el ayer,
lo que pudo ser y lo que no quiso ser.
Ya pasado el bosque de las ideas, se llega al lago.
Aguas profundas con sabor a decepción,
se agitan las palas y así entre muecas se empuja la barca.
Hasta en este lugar existen los malditos mosquitos,
lanzan sus estocadas cuando menos se esperan,
hacen sangrar con torturas pasadas,
y estrujan los nervios obligando a recordar.
Mas no debemos olvidar de donde son los condenados moscos:
Siguen siendo nosotros.
Así como pican, confunden.
Ya no sé si soy yo… ¿pero y si sí?
¿Es la auto-flagelación suficiente redención?
El resentimiento físico de la batalla mental se hace llegar.
Ataca de manera sutil pues comienza de a poco.
Mientras los brazos se entierran en el cojín,
los pies de atril saludan a los dedos engarrotados.
Así todos tensos quedan a la espera.
Bienvenida seas, señora incomodidad.
No es el desaliento común.
Es el odio de la carne,
una revuelta de las venas,
es una irrascable comezón mental.
Míralo como agitar una casa de abejas.
El saco de huesos se retuerce entre las sábanas al alba,
tambaleándose de un lado al otro sobre el colchón.
Suenan y resuenan los resortes como lloriqueos por su estrés mecánico.
Así, entre quejidos del cuerpo,
se expresa el deseo de escapar,
mas no debemos olvidar la mente.
Ya sólita se comenzó a mutilar,
aun así, no desea levantarse.
No son adversarios;
sin embargo, no se puede llorar hacia adentro.
Está empapada de decepción.
Gracias al peso extra es inevitable sentirse presa,
¡mírala cómo se esconde y cómo huye!
pero algo en ella sabe:
durante la desesperación,
el cuerpo acecha con una carnívora intención.
¡Por fin están de acuerdo en algo estos dos!
Los pies llegan al suelo.

Unsweetened-Freedom.title: Unsweetened Freedom
Unsweetened-Freedom.content:
Human freedom is undeniable. We may argue about constraints and conditions that inevitably influence and even limit our capacity of choice. These constraints could also be an active, consciously-made choice by the agent (decision maker) in order to achieve something. It could also be some external force outside of their control. Yet, freedom is still there, even if consequences seem likely to happen, the choice is still ours.
Trying to deny one’s freedom is to say that we do not have control of our actions. In other words, that we are nothing but the mannequins of an unpredictable environment with no means of actions, just reactions. Animals are not self-aware the same way we are. Unlike other animals, humans are specially burdened by their own reflectiveness: we do not only act, but we also know that we are acting. The animal doesn’t attain self-awareness even if its safety is clear and needs are covered. In the same way, a human doesn’t suddenly lose its freedom when trapped behind bars or pressed by the responsibility of school or family. It can surely be constrained but freedom is still present. You are as free as an inmate is in jail.
This concept can be misunderstood very easily, because, How can an inmate be as free as me?
The idea of freedom doesn’t limit itself to the amount of possibilities that we have available, freedom is the capacity of choice. If this wasn’t true, there would be no need for guards to exist in prison. Inmates are still free, but an external agent is limiting the choices that they have available. Their freedom is limited but not completely revoked. They can still choose to get into a brawl during recreation hours, as well as they can choose to work out during bedtime. The same applies to those outside the cage.
You may wake up every day, go to work, come back, sleep, and repeat. How is this different from the routine an inmate has? The only difference is that we have a lot more options to choose from each day, although we already have boxed ourselves into a small array of possibilities just to eliminate the dread that freedom provokes upon us.
Through choices, people create the constraints necessary for them to block their perceived freedom, almost trying to deny or reduce it to: “I’m not completely free!” , where freedom is denied in some instances but celebrated in others. This simulated ignorance is what keeps us in the comfort zone where life becomes a big set of steps or hypothetical imperatives 1 where we do not care about finding value in the recognition of our capacity to choose. I do not blame them, it is natural for everyone to avoid looking into the abyss; a place with endless possibilities where you realize that any option is an option.  The product of this awareness is anxiety.
Anxiety happens when we look into an interminable number of options and realize that all of them are available. It is necessary for our existence to accept some options as predetermined---default responses to common situations, things like the process of washing dishes, how to drive a car safely, eating without biting your tongue off. All of these may seem as dumb examples, but they actually are the ones that propose the greatest anxiety.  When washing dishes, through experience you already decided that you grab a knife from the handle, or to not squeeze a cup of glass too much. Still, you are free to stab yourself or to smash the cup onto your head, that is still an option. Could you imagine having to decide how to do these things every single time you do them? Although we are free, we still must rely on certain decisions in order to avoid the dread. It is easy to imagine how stressful life would be to eat while actively trying to avoid eating your own tongue.
You may not experience anxiety in these cases because of the mechanisms that we evolved with. These practical habits are the things that we learn through experience to do. It allows us to avoid wasting unnecessary resources thinking about minor details of existence. These are a type of shade that we create in order to have a more pleasant life. The problem  lies in the fact that the anxiety that exists from mere habitual existence is---in the big scheme of things---the same type of dread that we face about other decisions.
It becomes a habit to wake up every day, commute to work, come back, sleep, and repeat. Just like stabbing yourself is still an option, skipping work is also an option. People hide themselves behind structure, they may value what they do every day, but most of the time they do not stop to question what they actually value. They might think that their six-figure job is valuable, but they think so just because is what society believes to be precious.2 This existential avoidance is a cowardly way of living where the agent fails to recognize their ability to freely choose just to run away from the dread of facing freedom.
Practical habits protect the mind from unnecessary decision-making. Existential avoidance occurs when a person uses structure not to merely function, but to avoid the responsibility and weight of their choices. If such structure is removed, we are left facing freedom directly. If we are to remove all those things that provide a sense of stability, we are left with the raw shape of our free life. Although structure essentially hides it, freedom is always present but masked. It is the removal of that mask and our inability to act upon it that brings a profound feeling of dread and despair.
This is the reason why breaks can become dark times for many. The level of dread that one may experience upon this tension is directly related to how aware the individual is of its own freedom. You definitely can surrender to a level of existence where you do whatever others suggest for you, but this would not help you feel fulfilled, just entertained.
Although structure itself is not inherently bad, the simulated ignorance of one’s life can become a point of crisis. Moreover, learning to live without a structure is a challenge that must be faced. Even if the individual is aware of his structure and find fulfillment in it, he still needs to find happiness outside of it. Breaks reveal the burden of self-direction by pushing a person to do the things that he likes but using only his will and desire, knowing that if he does or does not do so nothing will happen. There are no societal consequences to his actions, but there is a personal disappointment with oneself. This quieter and forceful punishment comes from the inside. The inner judge knows the values the individual claims to hold, and it punishes him when those values remain unchosen.
The dread of breaks is not just mere boredom, laziness, or lack of entertainment. It is the exposure to unsweetened freedom: the individual realizes that he is responsible for pursuing his interests. There are no external demands for his participation in life and the world remains indifferent to his actions, yet the individual remains responsible for pursuing what he claims to value. The individual becomes, at the same time, judge, jury, and executioner.
Footnotes


Immanuel Kant explains the Hypothetical imperative as a set of steps that do not apply at all times in all cases but rather an active choice dependent of the circumstances; “If I want X, then I must do Y.” In other words, if you will an end, you must will the means necessary to achieve it. ↩


With this, I’m not saying that a job is not really important or valuable. Is more a question of society’s-induced value into personal life vs real personal value. You may value your six-figure job because you find it purposeful or meaningful, the same way you could  “value” it just because it is a six-figure job. ↩

index.title: Welcome!
index.content:
Borradores para Máquinas y Pájaros
This is my personal blog: a place for notes, unfinished ideas, project logs, and more formal essays.
There is no specific topic here. Some posts may be about math, programming, engineering, books, tools, music, or reflections. The point is to avoid having everything perfectly organized and allow them to connect naturally.
Over time, I might separate more developed pieces from logs, short entries, and rants. For now, this site is a public notebook.
It is likely that some posts will be made in English while others in Spanish, because of this, I invite you to use the translation tool of the web browser you are using.

Less-serious-notes/Parametric-equations-.title: Parametric equations and Python. The failure of a sphere
Less-serious-notes/Parametric-equations-.content:
My intention was to create a sphere in python using the Manim library. In order to create it I needed to find a set of parametric equations that were able to escribe a sphere using parameters.

u: angle in radians around the z pole and
v: describing the distance in the z axis
I tried using x(u)= \sin(u)\cos(u) and y(u)= \cos(u). Then, to describe the change in height from the xy-plane, z(v)=\cos(v). Very surprisingly, it worked.
See image below of a diagram describing more or less the intended motion.



As I said before, it didn’t quite work.
I realized that simply using the 2 dimensional version of a parametric circle1 would now work because as our distance from the xy-plane increases, the radius of each circle decreases. I might be understanding or reasoning this in the wrong way but in my head it did make sense. The problem is that if we input \pi values [0,2\pi] it may appear that if we start from the top and we supposed both parameters u and v ‘advance’ at the same rate, it would work.
Since I barely started learning to use Manim2 today and I had not done much on python in the last 10 months, I was pretty rusty and it was tedious to find my way around. Eight very fun and very ‘well’ spent hours on creating this thing…
I just love solving problems that don’t exist…
I’m not completely sure of why I believed this would work in my head, it might be the mental fatigue but it was very fun to just believe* that it would work!, Below is the code that created the weird shape that even if it wasn’t the one I intended, I found it interesting since it threw me back to a flashback of me doing a lab at 9:00 pm at the Love Library!

from manim import *
import numpy as np
class NapkingRing(ThreeDScene):
 
def construct(self):
Camera1 = self.set_camera_orientation(
phi= 90 * DEGREES,
theta= -45*DEGREES
)
axes= ThreeDAxes()
AxesLabels = axes.get_axis_labels(
x_label = "x",
y_label = "y",
z_label = "z"
)
radius=1
height=2
res = 5
cylinder = Surface(
lambda u, v: np.array([
radius * np.cos(u),
radius * np.sin(u),
v,
]),
u_range= [0,TAU],
v_range = [-height/2 , height/2],
resolution=[res,res]
)
sphere = Surface(
lambda u, v: np.array([
radius * np.cos(u),
radius * np.sin(u)*np.cos(u),
radius * np.cos(v),
]),
u_range= [0,TAU],
v_range = [0, TAU],
resolution=[res,res]
)
cylinder.set_color(RED)
self.begin_ambient_camera_rotation()
self.add(AxesLabels, axes, sphere)
#self.play(Create(cylinder).set_run_time(4))
#not currently using "cylinder"
#self.wait(5)
Footnotes


The two-dimensional parametric circle can be described with the following set of parametric equations:
x = cos(u)
y = sin(u) ↩


I will talk about Manim later. If you want to see what is Manim capable of creating, go check out the 3Blue1Brown YT channel!! (P.S: He actually created Manim!) ↩
